parties:
Debishahar Agricultural & Fish Farming Co-Operative Society Ltd ----- Appellant
Vs. 
Narayan Chandra Swarnakar & others ----- Respondents
full_judgment: 2. The crucial question is in the facts and circumstances of the case whether the excess land is retainable in view of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The owners made an endeavour for a certificate under section 20(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act so that they could retain possession of the land beyond the prescribed limit for the purpose of large scale farming on co-operative basis. Such certificate was granted by the Revenue Officer but the Member, Board of Revenue cancelled the certificate in 1963. He took the view that the application of the Co-Operative Society was a mere camouflage to retain the excess land. The owners challenged the order of Board of Revenue by filing a Writ Petition being Writ Petition No. 168 of 1964. This petition was dismissed in January, 1966 and further appeal before the Supreme Court of Pakistan was also without any success. The owners then formed a Co-Operative Society and filed a title suit being T.S No. 441 of 1966 for permanent injunction to restrain the Government for interfering with their excess land and allotting the same to any other person. Their main contention was that on co-operative basis they have undertaken to do large scale farming. The Trial Court granted temporary injunction on 15.6.66. Thereafter an interesting episode took place Proforma defendant No. 4 Basanta Kumar Swarnakar died on 29.11.72. As his son was not substituted as an heir, the son filed an application under Order 1, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure to be added as a party to the suit. This application was rejected by the learned Subordinate Judge on 22.6.74. Thereafter a revisional application was filed being Civil Revision No. 1110 of 1974. Curiously enough, in that revision which is still pending before the High Court Division all further proceedings of the main suit were stayed. It is inconceivable how in a proceeding under Order 1, rule 10 all further proceeding in the suit could be stayed. That was highly irregular but it seems nobody took the trouble of rectifying the wrong, not even the Government. Then came the Martial Law on 24th March, 1982. It appears the plaintiff himself filed an application in the High Court Division for an order of 'status quo' in order to restrain the Government from disturbing the plaintiff's possession of the suit land. This petition gave rise to Civil Rule No. 32(R) It is to be noted that the temporary injunction that was granted on 15th June, 1966 was still continuing The reasons for moving the High Court Division for a status quo order can only be understood in the light of M.L.O. No. 14 of 1980 which barred the jurisdiction of the Court for granting restrictive order under certain circumstances. It seems it was the preemptive step by the plaintiff himself for asking for a status quo order. This prayer for status quo order was rejected by the courts below and the High Court also took the view that in view of the provision of M.L.O. No. 14 such order could not be passed.
